questions.question: 1. What is 'uplink' in a cellular system?

answers.a: The communication from the base station to the mobile phone.
answers.b: The communication from the mobile phone to the base station.
answers.c: The communication between two mobile phones directly.
answers.d: The communication from the base station to the central network.

questions.question: 2. An 'interfering user' in an uplink scenario is...

answers.a: a base station on the same frequency.
answers.b: a mobile phone in a different cell on the same frequency, whose signal is picked up by your base station.
answers.c: a mobile phone in your own cell on a different frequency.

questions.question: 3. What is the primary purpose of the 'vertical beam pattern' of a base station antenna?

answers.a: To control the signal strength in the horizontal (left-right) direction.
answers.b: To change the frequency of operation.
answers.c: To control the signal strength in the vertical (up-down) direction.
answers.d: To make the antenna physically taller.

questions.question: 4. If a base station's antenna has *no* downtilt, where is its main reception lobe (for uplink) pointed?

answers.a: Directly at the ground beneath the tower.

questions.question: 5. By applying downtilt, a base station's antenna focuses its reception. What is the effect on the *uplink* SINR for a user *within* the cell?

answers.a: It can improve SINR by reducing interference received from distant co-channel users.
answers.b: It always makes the SINR worse by reducing the desired signal.
answers.c: It has no effect on the uplink, only the downlink.

questions.question: 6. A mobile phone at the cell edge must use 'power control'. Why is this important for *uplink* SINR?

answers.a: It must transmit with *less* power to avoid interfering with its own base station.
answers.b: It must transmit with *more* power to ensure its signal is received, but not so much that it badly interferes with other cells.
answers.c: It must change its frequency to avoid interference.
answers.d: It must aim its signal upwards, matching the base station's tilt.

questions.question: 7. How does a base station's antenna *gain* (due to its beam pattern) affect the 'desired signal' in the uplink SINR calculation?

answers.a: It doesn't; only the mobile phone's power matters.
answers.b: The base station's gain in the direction of the mobile phone *amplifies* the received desired signal.
answers.c: It only amplifies the noise, not the signal.
answers.d: It only amplifies the interference, not the signal.

questions.question: 8. How does the same antenna gain (from beam tilt) affect the 'interference' component in the uplink SINR calculation?

answers.a: It amplifies the interference received from co-channel users based on their direction.
answers.b: It has no effect on interference.
answers.d: It only affects the desired signal.

questions.question: 9. If a base station's downtilt is *too small* (e.g., pointed at the horizon), it will likely receive strong interference from:

answers.a: Users who are very close to the tower.
answers.b: Users who are very far away in other cells.
answers.c: Other base stations (this is a downlink issue).

questions.question: 10. In the uplink SINR, what happens if the 'interference' component is much larger than the 'desired signal' component?

answers.a: The connection quality will be very good.
answers.b: The base station will easily understand the mobile phone's data.
answers.c: The connection will be poor, and the base station will struggle to understand the mobile phone's data.
answers.d: The noise level will automatically decrease to compensate.
